children: Joyce brings the romantic clichés to an extreme, and imbues the description with something beyond the clichés they expose – instead of being a mockery of the cliché and therefore a mockery of the characters, the language itself is shown to be hollow but the characters manoeuvre within it, push outside of it, and become real characters in their own right. Contrast with the use of clichés in Beckett’s
Murphy
where clichés are rolled out to sneer at the characters and their petty foibles.
This is typical of Joyce’s appropriation of language, cant, phrases and clichés.

children: Refers to a famous episode from Greek myth. As the
Vermont Apples
website for some reason explains:

Minerva (Athena) was the goddess of wisdom, but on one occasion she did a very foolish thing; she entered into competition with Juno (Hera) and Venus (Aphrodite) for the prize of beauty. It happened thus: At the marriage of Peleus and Thetis all the gods were invited with the exception of Eris (Discord). Enraged at her exclusion, the goddess threw a golden apple among the guests, with the inscription, “For the Fairest.” Thereupon Juno, Venus, and Minerva each claimed the apple. Jupiter (Zeus), not willing to decide in so delicate a matter, sent the goddesses to Mount Ida, where the beautiful shepherd Paris was tending his flocks, and to him was committed the decision.

The goddesses accordingly appeared before him. Juno promised him power and riches, Minerva glory and renown in war, and Venus the fairest of women for his wife, each attempting to bias his decision in her own favor. Paris decided in favor of Venus and gave her the golden apple, thus making the two other goddesses his enemies. Under the protection of Venus, Paris sailed to Greece, and was hospitably received by Menelaus, king of Sparta. Now Helen, the wife of Menelaus, was the very woman whom Venus had destined for Paris, the fairest of her sex….Paris, aided by Venus, persuaded her to elope with him, and carried her to Troy, whence arose the famous Trojan war, the theme of the greatest poems of antiquity, those of Homer and Virgil. The apple of this story is the “Apple of Discord” and describes any action or situation that causes dissension and turmoil that is more trouble than it is worth.

8630763.twitter_share_message: “The phrase “the memory of the past” alludes to a line in the song There Is a Flower That Bloomet…” —@Genius

children: The phrase “the memory of the past” alludes to a line in the song
There Is a Flower That Bloometh
in Wallace’s opera
Maritana
. The significance of references to “flowers”, and, of course, especially to “
Bloom
eth” in the novel suggests a special significance to Joyce here. Perhaps it is to his lingering regrets for the turn his life took early on as he recreates it for Stephen in
Portrait of the Artist
. There on Sandymount Strand, the same setting as in
Nausicaa
, (“[Young Stephen] looked northward toward Howth,” the promontory the narrator mentions six times in
Nausicaa

), Stephen wonders, “Where is my boyhood now?  Where was the soul that had hung back from her destiny, to brood alone upon the shame of her wounds and in her house of squalor and subterfuge… Or where was he?”
When Stephen is described in
Portrait
as “alone amidst… the veiled grey sunlight and gayclad figures of children and girls and voices and girlish in the air,” the similarities to
Nausicaa
could not be starker. The girl he is captivated by is described thusly: “Her long slender bare legs were delicate… Her thighs, fuller and soft-hued as ivory, were bared almost to the hips… Her
slate-blue

skirts were kilted boldly about her waist… But her long fair hair … touched, with wonder of mortal beauty, her face.” The narrator continues, “ She was… gazing out to sea; and when she felt his presence and the worship of his eyes, her eyes turned to him in quiet sufferance of his gaze…”

This moment radically transformed Stephen’s outlook, and led to a life of indulgence it is possible he came to deeply regret, and which may have contributed greatly to the sadness Gerty saw in Bloom’s face. That period of Stephen’s life, “[he] bore cynically with the shameful details of his secret riots in which he exulted to defile with patience whatever image had attracted his eyes.” Now, mature Bloom, despite whatever remorse he may feel, was about to defile the image that had attracted his eyes, the image he had nearly deified,with a secret, conscience-betraying act Stephen had habituated during, and despite, his virtue-seeking youth.

The memory of the past
― James Joyce – Ulysses (Chap. 13 - Nausicaa)

Used during laundering, it adds a trace of blue dye (often synthetic ultramarine, sometimes Prussian blue) to the fabric. White fabrics acquire a slight color cast after use (usually grey or yellow). It is also a colour associated with the Blessed Virgin.
